apple-developer-account.title: Join the Apple Developer Program
apple-developer-account.summary: Enroll in Apple's Developer Program so your app can be published on the App Store — it costs $99 per year.
apple-developer-account.clockNote: Apple activation takes 24-48h after payment — start this first, before anything else.
apple-developer-account.instructionsMarkdown:
1. You need an **Apple ID** with two-factor authentication turned on. If you don't have one, create it at https://appleid.apple.com. Keep the phone that receives your Apple verification codes nearby — you'll need it again later.
2. Go to https://developer.apple.com/programs/enroll/ and sign in with your Apple ID.
3. Choose **Individual / Sole Proprietor** enrollment (fastest — no paperwork).
   - ⚠ Individual enrollment shows **your personal name** as the seller on the App Store. If you want a company name shown instead, you must enroll as an Organization, which requires a D-U-N-S number and takes much longer.
4. Fill in your legal name and address exactly as they appear on your ID, and pay the **$99/year** fee by card.
5. You'll get a confirmation email. Your account is usually active within **24-48 hours** of payment.
   - ⚠ Don't worry if things look broken during this window — build errors about "credentials" in the first two days are almost always just Apple still activating your account.
6. Once active, you can sign in at https://developer.apple.com/account — if you see your membership listed there, you're done.
apple-developer-account.verifyHints: You're done when https://developer.apple.com/account shows an active 'Apple Developer Program' membership under your name. Note your 10-character Team ID (shown on that page under Membership details) — you'll need it later.

play-console-account.title: Create your Google Play Console account
play-console-account.summary: Set up the Google account that will publish your app on Google Play — a one-time $25 fee.
play-console-account.clockNote: New personal accounts must run a closed test with ~12 testers for 14 consecutive days before they can publish publicly — that clock is the real launch bottleneck, so start today.
play-console-account.instructionsMarkdown:
1. Pick ONE Google account and use it for **everything Google** in this wizard (Play Console, Google Cloud, Firebase). Mixing accounts is the #1 cause of confusing permission errors later.
2. Go to https://play.google.com/console/signup and sign in with that account.
3. Choose **Personal** account type (unless you have a registered business), fill in your details, and pay the **$25 one-time** fee.
4. **Identity verification**: Google will ask you to verify your identity (ID document and/or payment card). Follow the prompts — this can take minutes to a few days.
5. **Device verification**: Google requires you to prove you have an Android device.
   - Install the **Play Console app** from the Play Store on an Android phone, and sign in with the **same Google account** that owns the Console.
   - ⚠ No Android phone? Borrowing any Android phone for 10 minutes is the reliable path — you only need access, not ownership. Install the Play Console app, sign in, complete verification, then sign out and remove the app.
6. **The 14-day rule** (new personal accounts only): before your app can go live publicly, Google requires a **closed test with about 12 opted-in testers running for 14 consecutive days**. You'll recruit testers (friends and family work) once your first build is uploaded.
   - ⚠ This 14-day clock only starts once testers have opted in — start it as soon as device verification passes. Your iOS launch does not have to wait for it.
play-console-account.verifyHints: You're done when https://play.google.com/console shows your developer account dashboard with no pending verification banners.

expo-account-token.title: Create an Expo account and access token
expo-account-token.summary: Expo (free) is the build service that turns your app's code into installable iOS and Android apps under your own account.
expo-account-token.instructionsMarkdown:
1. Go to https://expo.dev/signup and create a free account (email + password is fine).
2. Verify your email address if Expo asks you to.
3. Sign in at https://expo.dev, then click your profile picture (top-right) → **Account settings**.
4. In the left sidebar, click **Access tokens** (direct link: https://expo.dev/settings/access-tokens).
5. Click **Create token**. Give it a name you'll recognize, like `app-publisher`, and create it.
6. **Copy the token immediately and paste it below.**
   - ⚠ The token is shown **only once**. If you lose it, delete it and create a new one — no harm done.
7. Also note your **Expo username** (shown under your profile) — the wizard may ask for it.
expo-account-token.verifyHints: A valid Expo access token is a long random string of letters, numbers and dashes (typically 30+ characters), with no spaces. It is NOT your password.

github-pat.title: Create a GitHub access token for your code
github-pat.summary: This read-only token lets the platform securely download your app's code from GitHub to build it — nothing more.
github-pat.instructionsMarkdown:
1. Sign in at https://github.com (create a free account at https://github.com/signup if you don't have one).
2. Go to https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens — this is under your profile picture → **Settings** → **Developer settings** → **Personal access tokens** → **Fine-grained tokens**.
3. Click **Generate new token**.
4. Fill in:
   - **Token name**: something like `app-publisher-read`.
   - **Expiration**: 90 days is fine (you can make a new one when it expires).
   - **Repository access**: choose **Only select repositories** and pick the repository that contains your app's code.
5. Under **Permissions** → **Repository permissions**, set **Contents** to **Read-only**. (GitHub will automatically add read-only "Metadata" — that's normal.) Leave everything else at "No access".
6. Click **Generate token**, then **copy it immediately and paste it below**.
   - ⚠ The token is shown **only once**. If you lose it, just generate a new one.
github-pat.verifyHints: A valid fine-grained token starts with `github_pat_` followed by a long string of letters and numbers, with no spaces.

asc-api-key.title: Create an App Store Connect API key
asc-api-key.summary: This key lets the platform upload builds to Apple for you, without ever needing your Apple password.
asc-api-key.clockNote: Requires your Apple Developer account to be fully activated (24-48h after payment).
asc-api-key.instructionsMarkdown:
1. Go to https://appstoreconnect.apple.com and sign in with the same Apple ID you used to enroll.
2. Click **Users and Access**, then open the **Integrations** tab (you may see it as "Keys" → "App Store Connect API").
3. Make sure you're on **Team Keys** (not Individual Keys).
4. Copy the **Issuer ID** shown at the top of this page — it's the first of three values you'll paste below.
5. Click the **+** button to generate a new key:
   - **Name**: something like `app-publisher`.
   - **Access (role)**: choose **App Manager** (or **Admin** — either works; App Manager is enough).
6. Click **Generate**. The new key appears in the list.
7. Click **Download API Key** next to it. This downloads a file named `AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8`.
   - ⚠ **You can download this file exactly ONCE — Apple never offers it again.** If you lose it, you must revoke the key and create a new one. Keep the file somewhere safe.
8. Note the **Key ID**: it's shown in the key list, and it's also the `XXXXXXXXXX` part of the downloaded filename `AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8`.
9. Paste all three values below: the **Issuer ID**, the **Key ID**, and the **contents of the .p8 file** (open it with any text editor — like TextEdit or Notepad — select all, copy, paste).
asc-api-key.verifyHints: The .p8 file content starts with `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----` and ends with `-----END PRIVATE KEY-----`. The Key ID is 10 characters (letters and digits). The Issuer ID looks like `57246542-96fe-1a63-e053-0824d011072a` (a UUID with dashes).

play-service-account.title: Create a Google service account for Play uploads
play-service-account.summary: This robot account lets the platform upload Android builds to your Play Console for you.
play-service-account.instructionsMarkdown:
1. ⚠ Do ALL of this signed in as the **same Google account** that owns your Play Console — being signed into a different Google account in the same browser is the classic cause of permission errors. If in doubt, use a private/incognito window.
2. Go to https://console.cloud.google.com. If asked, accept the terms. Create a new project (top bar → project picker → **New Project**), name it after your app, and select it.
3. In the left menu (☰), go to **IAM & Admin** → **Service Accounts** (direct: https://console.cloud.google.com/iam-admin/serviceaccounts).
4. Click **+ Create service account**. Name it `play-publisher`. Click **Create and continue**, skip the optional role and access screens, and click **Done**.
5. In the service accounts list, click your new account, open the **Keys** tab → **Add key** → **Create new key** → choose **JSON** → **Create**. A `.json` file downloads — keep it safe.
6. Copy the service account's **email address** (looks like `play-publisher@your-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com`).
7. Now grant it access in Play Console: go to https://play.google.com/console → **Users and permissions** → **Invite new user**.
8. Paste the service account email as the user's email address. Under permissions, grant it access to your app with at least: **View app information**, **Create and edit draft apps**, **Release to testing tracks**, and **Manage testing tracks**. (Granting the "Release manager" style permission set is the simple choice.) Click **Invite user** / **Send invitation**.
9. Open the downloaded `.json` file in a text editor, select all, copy, and **paste its full contents below**.
play-service-account.verifyHints: The pasted value is a JSON block starting with `{` that contains `"type": "service_account"`, a `"client_email"` ending in `.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, and a long `"private_key"` field containing `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----`.

app-identity.title: Choose your app's name and identifier
app-identity.summary: Pick the display name users will see and the permanent technical ID that identifies your app in both stores.
app-identity.instructionsMarkdown:
1. **App display name**: this is what appears under your icon and in the stores.
   - Must be **30 characters or fewer** (Apple's hard limit; keeping it short also looks better under the icon).
   - You CAN change the display name later, so don't agonize over it.
2. **Bundle ID / package name**: the technical identifier for your app, identical concept on iOS (bundle ID) and Android (package name).
   - Use **reverse-DNS style**: your domain (or name) backwards, plus the app. Examples: `com.janedoe.fittrack`, `com.mycompany.recipes`.
   - Rules: lowercase letters and dots only is safest. On Android, **hyphens are not allowed** and no segment may start with a digit. Avoid generic prefixes like `com.example`.
   - If you own a domain (e.g. `janedoe.com`), base it on that. If not, `com.<yourname>.<appname>` is fine — no one checks domain ownership.
3. ⚠ **The bundle ID is PERMANENT after your first upload to either store.** It can never be changed — a "rename" would mean publishing a brand new app and losing all users, reviews, and test history. Double-check spelling before continuing.
4. Enter both values below.
app-identity.verifyHints: Display name: 1-30 characters. Bundle ID: at least two dot-separated segments, all lowercase, letters/digits/dots only (e.g. `com.janedoe.fittrack`), no spaces, no hyphens, no segment starting with a digit.

android-install.title: Install the Android test build on your phone
android-install.summary: Install the APK file the platform produces directly on any Android phone — no store or registration needed.
android-install.instructionsMarkdown:
1. When your Android build is ready, the wizard shows a **download link**. Open that link in the browser **on your Android phone** (or scan the QR code if one is shown).
2. The phone downloads a file ending in **.apk**. Tap the download notification (or find it in your **Files/Downloads** app) and tap the file to install.
3. The first time, Android will block the install and show something like **"For your security, your phone is not allowed to install unknown apps from this source"**:
   - Tap **Settings** in that popup, then turn ON **Allow from this source** for your browser (the setting lives under Settings → Apps → your browser → **Install unknown apps**).
   - Go back and tap **Install**.
4. Google **Play Protect** may show a warning like "App scan recommended" or "Unsafe app blocked" because the app isn't from the Play Store yet. Tap **More details** → **Install anyway**. This is normal for test builds — it's your own app.
5. Open the app from your home screen and try it out.
   - ⚠ Unlike iOS, Android test builds install on **any** phone with no device registration — feel free to share the download link with friends who are helping you test.

ios-testflight.title: Install the iOS test build via TestFlight
ios-testflight.summary: Apple test builds are installed through TestFlight, Apple's official app for trying pre-release apps.
ios-testflight.clockNote: After the platform uploads a build, Apple takes 5-15 minutes of processing before it appears in TestFlight.
ios-testflight.instructionsMarkdown:
1. On your iPhone, install the free **TestFlight** app from the App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/testflight/id899247664.
2. After the platform uploads your iOS build, wait **5-15 minutes** — Apple processes every build before it becomes available.
3. Add yourself as a tester (one-time setup):
   - Go to https://appstoreconnect.apple.com → **Apps** → your app → **TestFlight** tab.
   - Under **Internal Testing**, click **+** to create a group (call it "Internal"), then add yourself as a tester using **your own Apple ID email**. (If your email isn't offered, add it first under **Users and Access** — internal testers must be members of your team.)
   - Enable **automatic distribution** for the group so every new build reaches you without extra clicks.
4. You'll receive an email titled roughly "You've been invited to test…". Open it **on your iPhone** and tap **View in TestFlight**, or open the TestFlight app and redeem the invitation.
5. In TestFlight, tap **Install** next to your app. From then on, TestFlight notifies you whenever a new build arrives — just tap **Update**.
   - ⚠ Internal testing needs **no Apple review** — builds are available as soon as processing finishes. Builds expire after 90 days, which is fine for testing.

google-signin-oauth.title: Enable Google Sign-In (optional)
google-signin-oauth.summary: Set up the Google credentials that let users log into your app with their Google account.
google-signin-oauth.instructionsMarkdown:
Google Sign-In credentials can only be created through Firebase (Google's app platform). Use the **same Google account** as your Play Console throughout.
1. Go to https://console.firebase.google.com and click **Create a project** (or "Add project").
   - If the wizard offers to use your **existing Google Cloud project** (the one from the service-account step), choose it — don't create a separate one. Accept the Firebase terms when asked.
   - You can decline Google Analytics — it's not needed.
2. In your Firebase project, click the **iOS+ icon** to add an iOS app. Enter your **bundle ID** exactly as chosen in the app-identity step. Register it (you can skip the config-file download steps for now — the platform fetches what it needs).
3. Click **Add app** again → **Android**. Enter your **package name** (same as the bundle ID). The platform will provide a **SHA-1 fingerprint** for your Android build — paste it into the SHA-1 field (you can also add it later under Project settings → your Android app → **Add fingerprint**).
4. In the left menu: **Build** → **Authentication** → **Get started** → **Sign-in method** tab → click **Google** → toggle **Enable** → set your support email → **Save**. This single step is what actually creates the sign-in credentials (OAuth clients).
5. Collect the values to paste below:
   - **Web client ID**: Firebase console → Authentication → Sign-in method → Google → expand **Web SDK configuration** → copy **Web client ID**.
   - **iOS client ID**: go to https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials (same project) — under **OAuth 2.0 Client IDs** copy the ID of the entry ending in "(iOS)" or created for your iOS app.
6. Fix the consent screen name: at https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/branding, change the app name — otherwise users see "project-xyz…" on the Google login popup. ⚠ This page only works for the project **owner** account. Changing the name is instant; adding a **logo** triggers a 2-5 day Google brand review that requires a verified website — skip the logo for now.
7. ⚠ After your app is later published on Google Play, one extra step: Play Console → **Test and release** → **App integrity** → copy the **App signing key SHA-1** and add it as a second fingerprint in Firebase (Project settings → Android app → Add fingerprint). Without it, Google Sign-In fails only in the store version — a confusing bug to hit later.
google-signin-oauth.verifyHints: Both client IDs end in `.apps.googleusercontent.com`. The web client ID and iOS client ID are different values — don't paste the same one twice. The iOS one is the client ID whose type/label says iOS.

apple-signin.title: Enable Sign in with Apple (optional)
apple-signin.summary: Set up the Apple key that lets users log into your app with their Apple ID (required by Apple if you offer Google Sign-In on iOS).
apple-signin.instructionsMarkdown:
Good news: the "Sign in with Apple" capability on your app is enabled automatically by the build platform. You only need to create one key — used to properly disconnect users' Apple accounts when they delete their in-app account (an App Review requirement).
1. Go to https://developer.apple.com/account/resources/authkeys/list and sign in.
2. Click the **+** button to create a new key. Name it something like `siwa-key`.
3. Check the box next to **Sign in with Apple**, then click **Configure** next to it.
4. Select your app as the **Primary App ID**. The picker shows entries like `ABCDE12345.com.janedoe.fittrack` — the 10-character prefix before the dot is your **Team ID**. Write it down; it's one of the values to paste below.
5. Click **Save**, then **Continue**, then **Register**.
6. Click **Download**. You get a file named `AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8`.
   - ⚠ **This download is offered exactly ONCE — Apple never re-issues it.** If you lose the file you must create a new key and reconfigure. Store it safely.
7. The **Key ID** is the `XXXXXXXXXX` part of the filename `AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8` (also shown on the key's page).
8. Paste the three values below: the **contents of the .p8 file** (open it in a text editor, copy everything), the **Key ID**, and the **Team ID**.
Note: a "Services ID" is only needed for Sign in with Apple on **websites** — your native mobile app does not need one.
apple-signin.verifyHints: The .p8 content starts with `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----`. The Key ID is 10 characters (letters and digits, matches the filename). The Team ID is 10 characters and matches the one shown at https://developer.apple.com/account under Membership details. Note: this is a DIFFERENT key from the App Store Connect API key — don't reuse that one.

backend-hosting.title: Where your app's data lives (backend)
backend-hosting.summary: Most apps built with Lovable already have their backend hosted — check which case applies to you.
backend-hosting.instructionsMarkdown:
Your app has two halves: the **app on the phone** (what ShipKit builds) and the **backend** — the server that stores accounts, data and logins.

1. **Built with Lovable?** Your backend is **Supabase**, and it is already hosted. The native conversion keeps it untouched: same project, same data, same logins. **There is nothing to deploy** — just keep access to your Supabase account (supabase.com).
   - ⚠ Keep *Row Level Security* enabled on your Supabase tables — it is what stops users from reading each other's data, and privacy regulators (GDPR) expect it.
2. **Custom API server?** (you or a developer wrote your own backend) — the next step deploys it to Google Cloud under your own account.
3. **Not sure?** The Overview tab shows what ShipKit detected, or ask the Chat: "What backend does my app use, and is it already hosted?"

Mark this step done once you know which case you are in.

gcp-deploy.title: Deploy a custom backend to Google Cloud (optional)
gcp-deploy.summary: Only if your app has its own API server — your AI agent deploys it to Cloud Run under your Google account, with no downloaded keys.
gcp-deploy.clockNote: Creating a Google Cloud account takes ~10 minutes; new accounts include free credits.
gcp-deploy.instructionsMarkdown:
**Skip this entirely if your backend is Supabase** (see the previous step).

1. Go to https://console.cloud.google.com and sign in. Use **ONE Google account** for everything Google (Cloud, Play Console, Firebase) — mixing accounts is the #1 cause of confusing permission errors.
2. Create a **new project** (top bar → project picker → New project). Note its **Project ID** (shown under the name — it can't be changed later).
3. Enable **billing** on the project (Menu → Billing). New accounts get free credits; a small API on the cheapest settings usually costs a few euros per month.
4. Install the **Google Cloud CLI** on this machine — Settings → *Your machine* shows the status and install steps. Then run `gcloud auth login` and `gcloud auth application-default login` in a terminal (each opens a browser to sign in).
5. Paste your Project ID below and save.
6. Open the **Chat** tab and ask: "Deploy my backend to Google Cloud Run, project <your-project-id>". The agent sets everything up **keyless** (no credential files on disk), runs the database migrations, and verifies the deployment health before reporting back.
   - ⚠ If a Google console page shows a permission error mentioning `resourcemanager.projects.get`, you are signed into the **wrong Google account** — switch accounts, don't change permissions.
gcp-deploy.verifyHints: Project IDs are 6–30 characters, lowercase letters/digits/hyphens (e.g. my-app-prod-4821).

store-icon.title: Your app icon (the source of everything)
store-icon.summary: One 1024×1024 icon drives every store visual — store icons, Android icon set, logos, favicon, feature graphic.
store-icon.instructionsMarkdown:
Every visual the stores need is derived from **one square icon**, ideally 1024×1024 pixels.

1. **Already have a logo?** Export it as a **1024×1024 PNG** (from Lovable, Figma, Canva…), name the file exactly `icon-source.png`, and drop it in the upload box below.
2. **No file at hand?** Your app probably already contains its logo — open the Chat and ask: "Find the best icon source in my app and tell me if it's good enough for the stores."
3. ⚠ **Never use a small image scaled up** — blurry icons get flagged by both stores. Bigger than 1024 is fine (it scales down cleanly); smaller is not.

Mark this step done once a good source exists.
store-icon.verifyHints: A square PNG, at least 1024×1024, on a solid or simple background — no screenshots, no text-heavy images.

store-screenshots.title: Take your 6 store screenshots
store-screenshots.summary: Screenshots ARE your store page — take up to 6 raw captures; ShipKit derives every required size from them.
store-screenshots.instructionsMarkdown:
Shoppers decide from screenshots. You take the raw captures (only you know what looks good); the AI turns them into every size the stores demand.

1. Install your app on a phone (Builds tab) — or use the simulator — and fill it with **nice-looking demo data** (real-looking names, a few entries, no empty screens).
2. Capture up to **6 screens**, in this story order (skip what doesn't apply — 4 is fine):
   1. Home — the first impression
   2. Your core flow — the thing the app is FOR
   3. Your differentiator — what competitors don't have
   4. Stats / progress — the payoff over time
   5. AI feature — if you have one
   6. Social / sharing — if you have it
3. Use the **biggest phone you have**, in **portrait**. Screenshots at full device resolution — don't compress or crop them yourself.
4. Drop them in the upload box below.
store-screenshots.verifyHints: PNG or JPG, portrait, straight from the device (no editing needed).

store-visuals-generate.title: Let the AI produce every store asset
store-visuals-generate.summary: The agent derives icon sets, resized screenshots and the Google Play feature graphic — everything lands in one folder.
store-visuals-generate.instructionsMarkdown:
1. Open the **Chat** tab and ask: **"Generate my store visuals."**
2. The agent produces, from your icon and raw screenshots:
   - **Icon set**: App Store icon (1024), the full Android adaptive set, OAuth consent logo (120×120), website/apple-touch icons, favicon.
   - **App Store screenshots** at 1284×2778 (the size Apple actually asks for at upload).
   - **Google Play screenshots** at 1080×2160.
   - **Play feature graphic** (1024×500) — required by Google Play with no iOS equivalent; it's the one everyone forgets. Composed from your icon and brand colors, never a stretched screenshot.
3. Everything lands in the `store-assets` folder of your project. Want changes? Just tell the chat in plain language: "make the feature graphic background darker", "use the tagline 'Train smarter'".

⚠ This uses your Mac's built-in image tools (`sips`) plus Python's Pillow — the agent checks both and tells you (with an Action card) if something's missing.
store-visuals-generate.verifyHints: Done when store-assets/ contains icons/, appstore/, play/ and feature-graphic.png.
